newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria re-opens its biggest synagogue.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria re-opens its biggest synagogue.

text.p: More than a thousand Jews from around the world gathered on Sunday to re-inaugurate Sofia synagogue, Bulgaria's biggest and one of the most ornate in Europe.
The lavish ceremony was attended by the speaker of Israel's parliament, the Knesset, Dan Tichon and Bulgaria's President Zhelyu Zhelev.
"I hope this temple, restored with great love and effort will also be a house of Jewish culture...not only a religious centre," said Tichon in a speech.

The 87-year-old copper-domed Moorish-style temple stands near both the central Sofia Mosque and another landmark, the St. Nedelia Orthodox Cathedral, reflecting Bulgaria's traditional religious tolerance.

The synagogue, designed by Austrian Architect Friedrich Grunander, was first inaugurated in 1909. It was hit by a bomb during World War Two and restoration was forbidden by the communist government until its fall in 1989.
The repairs, which will continue, have cost so far $370,000, most of it donated by the international Jewish community.

"The dark days of Nazism did not pass by this land. We, the Jews, will never forget that we were saved by the Bulgarian people who prevented the sending of thousands of Jews to the gas-chambers," said Tichon speaking through an interpreter.
Bulgaria's wartime government refused to hand over its 50,000 Jewish citizens to the Nazis in 1943 despite its military alliance with Germany.

The blowing of the "shofar" horn marked the beginning of a procession of seven leading members of the Bulgarian and International Jewish community each carrying a scroll of the Torah, or Jewish holy scrolls.
They walked up the aisles seven times as worshippers reached to touch the Torah.
They then put the scrolls inside the synagogue's five-metre (15-foot) tall Ark of the Covenant, a gilded marble cupboard, signifying that God had returned to the temple.
Religious services never stopped through the years, but were held in a meagre room adjoing the main hall of the synagogue, Rabi Avram Behar told Reuters.
There were 25,000 Jews and seven big synagogues in Sofia before the War. About 90 percent of the Jews emigrated to the newly-founded state of Israel afterwards.
"This is a victorious moment for Judaism, a long-awaited reward for all our efforts," said Behar.
